passage: At the bus stand outside Mahua, Deepak leaned against the tea stall and said loudly, "Vikas only got into the district hostel school because his uncle knows the headmaster." A few boys laughed. Vikas felt the words go in like a splinter. He had studied by lamp light for months, but he had also heard his uncle mention the headmaster once, and a small voice asked, what if it is partly true? He didn't argue. He bought his bus ticket and stared out of the window. That evening he went to his science teacher and asked, "Sir, was my selection fair? Do you think I can keep up?" The teacher told him the entrance marks were his own and gave him two areas to work on. Vikas felt lighter, and got out his notebook.

qa.q: Where did Deepak make his remark about Vikas?
qa.a: At the bus stand outside Mahua, by the tea stall.

qa.q: Why did the remark sting Vikas so much?
qa.a: Because he half-feared it might be partly true after remembering his uncle mention the headmaster, even though he had worked hard for months.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that was wise?
qa.a: He didn't argue, and let his work answer. He asked his science teacher for honest feedback and got specific areas to improve.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Vikas's silence at the bus stand?
qa.a: Possibly as an admission, or as a lack of reaction that takes away the fun of teasing. Deepak may also be jealous, but the passage does not say.

grounding: A rival sneers that the protagonist got in through favour; he lets his work answer and asks a mentor for honest feedback.

passage:
The selection trial for the district hockey squad was at seven, and it was pouring. Leela's bus had broken down near the flyover, so she ran the last kilometre with her stick wrapped in a plastic bag.

She arrived soaked and three minutes late. Preeti, stretching near the goal, didn't lower her voice. "Relax, she'll get picked anyway. Her mama is on the committee."

Leela felt it in her throat. The worst part was that she had wondered the same thing. Her uncle did sit on the committee. She hadn't asked him for anything, but maybe he had said something.

She had no time to argue, and she didn't try. She played the trial on a waterlogged pitch, went hard into every tackle, and kept her mouth shut.

Afterwards she walked up to Coach Rehana. "Ma'am, can you tell me honestly where my game is? Not what my family would want to hear." The coach looked at her for a long moment. "Your tackling is squad level. Your passing under pressure isn't yet. Work on that."

qa.q: What was Leela's stick wrapped in?
qa.a: Leela's stick was wrapped in a plastic bag.

qa.q: Why did Preeti's comment hurt Leela so much?
qa.a: It stung because Leela was already afraid it might be true, since her uncle did sit on the committee.

qa.q: Why was asking Coach Rehana for honest feedback a wise move?
qa.a: It gave Leela a fair measure of her game that did not depend on family ties, and showed her exactly what to work on.

qa.q: How might Preeti see Leela playing hard without arguing back?
qa.a: Preeti may feel her sneer did not land as she hoped, and may start to see Leela as a real competitor rather than a favourite.

grounding: It shows a teen stung by a rival's sneer that she got in through favour, who fears it may be true, lets her play answer and asks a mentor for honest feedback.

passage:
The notice went up on Monday: Sangeeta, editor, school magazine. By lunch, Mridul was holding court at the canteen counter.

"Obviously she got it. Her mother teaches chemistry here. Principal Sir loves her." He saw Sangeeta coming and grinned wider. "Congratulations, editor. Well connected."

Sangeeta paid for her samosa and walked away without a word, though her ears were burning. Mridul wasn't entirely stupid. She did sometimes wonder whether her mother's name had helped.

That evening in their flat in Lajpat Nagar, she sat staring at the three pieces she had submitted. Were they good, or just familiar?

The next day she went to Ms Fernandes, who ran the creative writing club and had never taught her mother's classes. "Please be blunt. Would you have picked me?" Ms Fernandes read the pieces again. "The travel essay, yes. The poem is weak. You're the editor because of the essay."

Sangeeta went home and started rewriting the poem. She didn't reply to Mridul's comments in the group chat.

qa.q: Where was Mridul standing when he made the comment?
qa.a: Mridul was at the canteen counter.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta's burning ears suggest?
qa.a: They suggest she felt humiliated and hurt, and partly afraid Mridul was right that her mother's name had helped.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta do that was wise?
qa.a: She asked Ms Fernandes, a mentor who had no link to her mother, for blunt feedback, then worked on the weak poem instead of arguing online.

qa.q: How does Mridul see Sangeeta's new role?
qa.a: Mridul seems to see it as unfair favouritism, perhaps because he wanted it himself, and uses sneers to make her doubt herself.

grounding: It shows a teen facing a rival's sneer that she only got a post through favour, fearing it might be true, asking a mentor for honest feedback and not feeding the argument.
